newsitem.title: INDIA: India political drama spotlights corruption's hold.
newsitem.headline: India political drama spotlights corruption's hold.

text.p: The resignation on Friday of a powerful Indian politician indicted in a multi-million dollar embezzlement scandal capped an agonising debate on corruption as this nation prepares to celebrate a half-century of independence.

Laloo Prasad Yadav, chief minister of Bihar state, resigned three months after he was indicted by federal investigators in the $280 million scandal that involved the alleged use of fictitious firms to siphon off state farm funds.
The Laloo Yadav crisis has triggered much navel-gazing about corruption, but little else.
Yadav's resignation overshadowed the swearing-in earlier on Friday of K.R. Narayanan as India's new president.
Narayanan wasted no time in echoing other old-school statesmen to say India was stalked by what independence leader Mahatma Gandhi called the "demon of corruption".

"Since Gandhiji uttered these prophetic and cautionary words, corruption has become widespread, violence has been erupting in almost walk of life, and values we have cherished are being eroded in an alarming manner," Narayanan said in his first speech as head of state.
"Excessive obsession with the pursuit of pure politics has often overshadowed the social, economic and developmental needs of the people," he said.
That candour did not take away from the helplessness of India's leaders in fighting Gandhi's demon.
Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral sounded a plaintive note in a recent television interview, saying: "Corruption, I can say with great regret, has seeped into the veins of the nation."
"I am not tolerating corruption but I have not discovered that magic wand where I can say 'no corruption' and there will be no corruption tomorrow," Gujral said.
Gujral said he had even given up on law enforcement agencies to cleanse the system.

"Let us understand that the police organisations are not what you would call pure, as though washed with milk," he said. "Those through whom you are trying to contain this (corruption) also have their difficulties."

Gujral is widely seen as a weak leader struggling to control an unruly coalition and his plaint sparked sharp criticism. "Such repeated declamations of helplessness can only demoralise the valiant few who are battling venality and graft in the face of gigantic odds," the Pioneer said in an editorial.

"Besides, Mr Gujral's track record on the issue does not exactly suggest helplessness," the daily said, referring to a government decision to abruptly transfer the federal police chief who had spearheaded investigations into the Bihar farm scandal.
Gujral's United Front itself was formed last year after the once-mighty Congress party suffered a crushing defeat in general elections, following a slew of corruption scandals.
In one case, more than half a dozen Congress government ministers resigned last year after being named in a money-laundering scandal.
Yadav resigned after a special court ordered his arrest, but won a brief reprieve when the country's Supreme Court said he could not be detained until July 29 when it heard his appeal.
Political analysts said Yadav's case was a symptom of a sickness that has gnawed at the entrails of the world's second most populous nation.

Independent analyst Rasheed Talib said corruption was endemic in India because employees in its sprawling bureacracy were poorly paid and the private sector was scrambling to find uses for money that it did not declare to tax authorities.
"When the bureaucratic pipeline is so long, there are bound to be leakages," Talib told Reuters.

"Part of the problem is the electorate doesn't take it seriously either -- the common voter thinks either that every politician is corrupt or that corruption isn't all that wrong. All these politicians are tarred by the same brush," he said.
